# Failure analysis: what the eval says, and what to do about it

*Written after the P3 runs. Every number here is in [`docs/results/eval.md`](../results/eval.md) or [`docs/results/failures.md`](../results/failures.md), both generated by script from `runs/evals/`. It covers the test split unless it says otherwise. The customer and its data are fictional.*

## The short version

- **Sonnet 5 finds 93.5% of order lines exactly (right product, right quantity) on the synthetic test set, and gets 72.7% of orders exactly right.** Fuzzy matching, which is today's fallback when the API is down, gets 56.4% and 20.7%.
- **The customer's own order history matters more than which model reads the message.** Removing history and nicknames drops Sonnet from 92.5% to 56.2% of lines on the same 100 conversations. Switching Sonnet for Haiku costs 4.6 points.
- **The hand-written set is harder than the generated one:** 80.5% of lines found and 60.0% of orders exactly right. Most of the gap comes from one thing the generator never modelled: what "box" and "packet" mean depend on the product (below).
- **Nothing should be auto-confirmed on this evidence.** The confidence model would wave through 38% of lines at a 1% error budget, and 85% at 2%. Both numbers rest on a threshold picked on synthetic data, and the 1% tier is a few hundred lines thick, so one refit can move it a lot. That is a reason to run shadow mode, not a reason to switch auto-confirm on.

## Where the errors are

Sonnet makes 138 line errors on the test split. Tracing each one to the step that lost it ([`failures.md`](../results/failures.md), "Which step lost the line"):

| Step | Errors | What it means |
|---|---:|---|
| Choice | 85 | The right product was among the candidates; the model picked another, or none. |
| Quantity or unit | 31 | Right product, wrong number or wrong pack level. |
| Extra line | 14 | The draft has something nobody ordered. |
| Retrieval | 7 | The line was read, but the right product wasn't offered. |
| Reading | 1 | The line wasn't extracted at all. |

The interesting result is the one that *isn't* there: retrieval almost never loses the line. Deterministic candidate generation (aliases, fuzzy matching, the customer's history) is doing its job. The errors are judgement calls the model makes between candidates it was given.

## Patterns, with examples

### 1. Gulf and South Asian shop vocabulary the model reads the wrong way (choice)

These come from the held-out names (88.7% right versus 93.1% for names in the alias table) and from Arabizi (85.7%):

- **"3aish masri"** is *Egyptian rice* in Gulf usage. In Egypt, عيش means bread, and the model read it as bread (test-004).
- **"6aqa"** (طاقة, energy) is an energy drink. The model read it as water (test-123) and as laban (test-233).
- **"mai ghazi"** (ماء غازي) is sparkling water. The model went looking for a brand called "Ghazi" (test-178).
- **"6a7een"** (طحين) is flour. The model read it as *tahini* (test-025).
- **"lait"** means *light*, as in diet. The model didn't recognise it in "lait bu6el 9gheer" or "lait 6" (test-168, test-256).

**What fixes it is not a bigger prompt.** These words are held out of the alias table on purpose, to measure exactly this. In production they become learned aliases: the console's "teach this name" button writes the alias after one correction, and retrieval uses it for every customer from then on. Week 2 seeds the table from the client's real order history ([week-2 plan](week-2-plan.md)).

### 2. Size left out (choice), now fixed in code

When a retailer writes "tuna fish" with no size and has only ever bought the 85 g tin, the answer is the 85 g tin. The resolve prompt says so. The model still picked a "common size" in 15 such cases in the first run, for example "lemon soda dait" → 150 ml can, for a customer who had bought the 2.25 L bottle 31 times.

**Fix:** when no size is written and the customer's history has exactly one size of the chosen product, code uses it and flags the line `size_from_history`. It fired on 17 test lines, 16 of them right, and the size-left-out slice is now 94.7%. The reasoning: the model is good at *which product*, and code is better at *which of their usual sizes*. This is the same split as ADR 0001.

### 3. Size or price read as a quantity (quantity)

"12 bori masoor dal 5" became 5 sacks instead of 12 (test-062), and "a shrink crunchos ketchup 15" became 15 packs (test-100). The extraction prompt already has an example of this trap, so a prompt change alone is unlikely to remove it.

**Mitigation:** the quantity guard. A line asking for more than 3× the most the customer ever ordered of that product is flagged for a look. On the test split it flags 35 Sonnet lines, of which 5 are wrong, and those 5 carry 27% of the value at risk. On the fuzzy fallback it catches 88% of the value at risk, because fuzzy matching reads "450 g" as 450 cartons. The guard matters most exactly when the model is down.

### 4. Removing something from a repeat order (extra line), now fixed in code

"Same as last order but anda brown nahi chahiye" (no brown eggs) left the brown eggs on the draft (test-036). The resolve step answered NONE, with the reason "this is a negation/exclusion, not an order for a product". The resolve prompt never says that a removal needs a product too. So there was nothing to remove. **Fix:** a removal can only drop something on the order. If the model named another size, or abstained, code removes the one order line in that product family, using the model's pick or the top three retrieval candidates, and the draft says so in a note. It fired on 6 test conversations, and all 6 are now exactly right. A first version also fired in the whole-catalogue ablation, where the "top candidates" are just the start of the catalogue, and removed a cola for "no milk". It now only uses ranked retrieval candidates. The prompt-level fix (telling the resolver that removals need a product too) waits for the next paid run, so it can be measured on its own.

### 5. Units that depend on the product (hand-written set)

The biggest error class on the hand-written set is the pack level:

- "karak premix 4 boxes" means 4 retail boxes of 10 sachets, not 4 cartons.
- "cheeni 2 kg 5 packet" means 5 two-kilo bags.
- "خبز عربي كبير ١٠ ربطات" means 10 bags of bread.

The extraction prompt maps *box* to carton and *packet* to pack. That is right for cans of cola and wrong for anything sold as a box or a bag. **The fix belongs in code with the catalogue's packaging data:** keep the customer's unit word verbatim and resolve it against the product's own base unit. It is deliberately **not** done yet. The hand-written set is the closest thing this project has to real messages, and tuning on it would spend the last honest number. Week 2 makes the change and measures it on real shadow-mode messages.

### 6. One-off failures the pipeline now survives

- One reply out of 300 degenerated into 388 lines with no product (test-239).
- One reply came back with no intent (gold-24).

Validation rejected both, as designed, and the order went to a person. The extraction step now retries once with the validation errors as the reason, and a second bad answer still goes to a person.

## What the fixes bought, and how far to trust it

Three changes, all in code, no prompt changed: size from history, removals that drop what's on the order, one retry. Because the model calls were cached, the same outputs were re-measured with the new code for the cost of the retries alone.

| | Lines correct | Orders exactly right |
|---|---|---|
| Sonnet test, first run → after fixes | 93.8% → 95.0% | 66.0% → 72.7% |
| Sonnet dev, first run → after fixes | 94.3% → 95.4% | 69.2% → 74.2% |
| Sonnet hand-written set, first run → after fixes | 83.8% → 82.2% | 60.0% → 60.0% |

The line-level gain on test is significant (McNemar p = 3.7e-09; no line got worse), and the removal fix adds to orders exactly right without changing that test, because it removes extra lines, but **it is not a clean holdout**: the errors behind the fixes were read on these same sets. The hand-written set doesn't improve. Its errors are the unit problem above, which none of the three fixes touch. The right way to confirm any of this is fresh messages, which is what shadow mode provides.

## Haiku or Sonnet?

| | Haiku 4.5 | Sonnet 5 |
|---|---|---|
| Lines correct (test) | 91.3% | 95.0% |
| Orders exactly right | 57.0% | 72.7% |
| Photos of handwritten lists, lines found | 77.0% | 88.2% |
| Cost per conversation | $0.0118 | $0.0214 |
| Most lines auto-accepted with ≤ 2% wrong | none | 85% |

**Sonnet.** The difference is about a cent per order. At the brief's volume, a few hundred orders a day, that is a few dollars a day, set against an order-taker's minutes per order and the cost of one wrong delivery. Haiku's confidence scores also don't separate right from wrong well enough to skip a look at any error budget under 3%. If cost mattered at much higher volume, the cheaper design would be Haiku for text and Sonnet for photos, measured first.

## What this changes in the plan

1. **No auto-confirm in the pilot.** Every order is confirmed by a person, as planned. The [rollout plan](rollout-plan.md) sets the evidence that would change that.
2. **The alias-learning loop is a core feature, not a nice-to-have.** Shop vocabulary is the largest error class, and it is local. No general model knows what one shop means by its own name for a product.
3. **Week 2 is about units and real messages.** Packaging-aware unit resolution, and measuring the hand-written-set gap on the client's own WhatsApp history.
